[[RunningHead]]

A Tribute to Frances Tustin

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode

28 Holland Park
London W11 3TA

Maria Rhode  

Frances Tustin died on 11 November 1994, at the age of 81. Someone said to me during her last illness, ‘I never had supervision from her, but she's always been a presence in my life.’ Those who came in contact with her found that the way they saw their work, and indeed their life, was lastingly transformed. Thinking of her, I am reminded of lines from Jon Stallworthy's poem ‘Credits’:

Whose eyes, from looking much

On the circumference

Of life beyond this life

Mirrored two worlds at once.*

She was born Frances Vickers in Darlington on 15 October 1913. Her father taught at primary school and was a lay preacher; her mother was a deaconess. Her early life is documented in Sheila Spensley's book on her work, the second book in the Routledge series on Makers of Modern Psychotherapy (Spensley, 1995); readers of this journal will recall Maria Pozzi's evocative interview (Pozzi, 1991). Frances was an only child whose life was suddenly and completely changed when her mother informed her that they were leaving her father. She and her mother spent the following years moving from one place to another. Before her parents’ separation she had been keenly interested in biology, which she hoped to read at university. Both parents transmitted to her the belief that the things that mattered were not necessarily those that the world thought important. I remember her talking about an autistic child who was using a particular talent in order to get a fuss made of him. ‘He must think that grown-ups are all mad,’ she said, ‘to be taking these monkey-tricks seriously instead of realizing what really matters.’

She trained as a teacher, and wrote her first book, A Group of Juniors, on latency children.

Interviews

Caroline Essenhigh Hansi Kennedy Joint Director of the Anna Freud Centre with Anna Freud and Clifford Yorke 1977-82 and Co-Director with Clifford Yorke 1982-8

CE: Tell me about Anna Freud.

HK: I think it is important to remember that there are two dimensions to Anna Freud. First of all she was a psychoanalyst, but she was also a teacher. It was her first profession and in some way she never stopped being a teacher. She always liked being with young people and liked the idea of having a training which would secure the future of child psychoanalysis. In particular, she liked the fact that it was an international training with students from other countries who would broaden the case of child analysis in the world. (This happened of course to Freud's theories but child analysis was still in its infancy.)

CE: On leaving Vienna, why did Anna Freud not take up the many invitations to the USA and settle there?

HK: Anna Freud liked living in England and also felt gratitude towards the country that enabled her father and a retinue of thirty people to immigrate in 1938. Many of her closest colleagues from Vienna had moved to the USA where child analysis was beginning to flourish after the war and mental health workers clamoured for psychoanalytic training. It was then that she received invitations to join them. I think it was particularly the Yale group that wanted Anna Freud to teach there.

CE: What do you think would have happened to child psychoanalysis if Hitler had not existed?

HK: It is a very interesting question. I think what would have happened is that psychoanalysis would probably have developed in Vienna and perhaps in London but not spread to the USA so quickly.

Psychotic Breakdown in Adolescence

Lut de Rijdt

Lut de Rijdt

Kapucijnenvoer 35-3000 Leuven
Belgium

Lut de Rijdt  

Adolescent breakdown; defence; psychotic functioning; psychotherapy.

This paper explores the choice of psychoanalytic psychotherapy as treatment for an adolescent boy experiencing a psychotic breakdown. Comment is given on the value of the approach when psychosis is seen as defensive against the developmental imperatives of adolescence. This approach is contrasted with the masking of symptoms occurring with a pharmacological approach where the dynamic underlying the conflict is not available for exploration by the patient. The example of a 17-year-old boy is given, demonstrating the move from psychotic functioning, via the recognition of the separateness of the other, to neurotic functioning.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Readers across the world will have been deeply saddened by the news last November of the death of Frances Tustin. Although we had always known of the range of her teaching and the generosity with which she undertook this, as letters poured in to the Tavistock Clinic the extent of her influence and the internationality of her loss became dramatically underlined. We recall her kindness and thoughtfulness in sending her two last papers to the Journal for our first Routledge issue in 1994. Today we are glad to publish Maria Rhode's tribute to Frances: we have much to mourn and much to celebrate in knowing her.

It is always a pleasure to publish ‘the next Anne Alvarez’. ‘Motiveless malignity: problems in the psychotherapy of psychopathic patients’ is the final version of a paper given and discussed in Italy, Oxford and London. In it the author points the differences between the states of mind and internal worlds of neurotic, borderline and psychopathic patients with reference to qualities of destructiveness. The implications for technique are fully and usefully discussed, together with the impact on the psychopathic patient of meeting him in his world — ‘the inner bleak emotional cemetery’.

Leslie Ironside tackles the important area of false allegations of abuse by a patient — an area vital for practitioners to think about and plan for. The differences between allegations which are clearly recognized in the network as transference issues and those which are not are outlined via case examples, and the impact of child abuse procedures on patient, network and — painfully — therapist and family are explored. It is a brave paper and, we feel, an issue which needs greater recognition and discussion within the child mental health field.

‘Eric: a traumatized child’ is a paper originally given by Pat Radford in San Francisco and later in London. In it she explores the impact of ongoing interpersonal violence on the development of a 3-year-old boy. His five times weekly analytic treatment over a three-year period is reviewed and the lasting effect of the violence on his personality and development assessed.

Adam PhillipsOn Flirtation, London: Faber, 1994226 pp., £14.99.

Peter Wilson

Peter Wilson

74 Dukes Avenue
London N10 2PU

Peter Wilson  

The title of this book may suggest something other than what is in it. The popular idea of flirtation is of a kind of frivolity and coquetry. No one, it may be said, takes flirtation seriously; nor, too, things like Kissing, Tickling and Being Bored, which is the title of Adam Phillips’ previous book. There is a danger from the outset that Adam Phillips invites us to set him aside and not take him seriously — titles such as these can all too easily be passed by in favour of weightier more reverential tones.

It may well be, in the very spirit of paradox that he cherishes, that this is what he both wants and does not want. There is no doubt that at one level he commands substantial respect. This is a remarkably profound book, beautifully and precisely written and filled with sharp and telling insights. It is a work of scholarship; it is anything but light and flippant. And, yet, at another level, there is a question about how far he wants the book to rest safely on the shelves of established academia. In his last chapter, he writes of the nineteenth-century poet John Clare, whose terror was of being appropriated and exploited through being seen and known. There is perhaps here, too, a similar sensibility. Quite persistently, it seems, Adam Phillips eschews being taken ‘seriously’, for fear that this might cramp his mobility. The very originality that makes this book so distinctive depends no doubt on his keeping himself apart and indeed always on the move — and it is in this respect that we can possibly reach an understanding of the gist of this book and its title.

Flirtation is not a superficiality. It is far more generative than it seems — and it consists of a certain kind of movement, of mental agility, that keeps alive a spirit of ambiguity and unpredictability (the oldest sense of the word, ‘to flirt’, is ‘to jerk lightly away’). Flirtation, as Adam Phillips defines it, ‘is the calculated production of uncertainty’; it is ‘the opposite of compromise in its unwillingness to settle for things’. It forever flinches away from ‘the cherished vocabulary of commitment’; through its process of deferral, its refusal to foreclose, it keeps open possibilities and alternatives. It sustains desire and exploits the ‘idea of surprise’. Flirtation ‘keeps the consequences going’.

Sheila SpensleyFrances Tustin, London: Routledge1995154 pp. £12.99 pb., £30 hb.

Carol Hughes

Carol Hughes

London SE5

Carol Hughes  

‘This book is not primarily a biography, but is about the distinguished contribution to the psychoanalytic investigation of autism which Frances Tustin has made,’ Sheila Spensley states in her introduction. It does indeed give us a brief, illuminating biography in which one gets glimpses of Frances Tustin's sunny and enthusiastic personality, as well as her emotional honesty. And it does indeed give a succinct precis and explanation of her original and creative formulations on autism, but it goes much further than this and is about a great deal more.

This slim volume (only 129 pages of text) is packed with a vast amount and range of material. Starting with details of Frances Tustin's childhood, adult life and professional development, it moves on to elucidate the controversies in thinking around autism, traces the development of child psychiatry, the development of ideas and theories of psychosis and autism in both adults and children, devotes two chapters to mental handicap and learning impairment and finishes with a chapter entitled ‘The restoration of God’.

The extent and scope of the subject matter covered is both the richness and challenge of this book. The writing is dense, packed with theories, information and ideas.

Frances Tustin's work and thinking are presented within the context of psychoanalytic and psychiatric thinking of the time. Thus, as a reader, besides attempting to understand the originality and scope of Tustin's work, one has to grapple with distillations of theories from Henry Maudsley, Baron-Cohen, Mahler, Bion, Bick, Klein, Ogden, Stern, Rutter, Wing, Meltzer, Winnicott and even quotes from The Madness of George III by Alan Bennett. I found myself wondering who the readership of this book would be.

Helen Bender

Helen Bender

London E1

Helen Bender  

‘The history of man for the nine months preceding his birth would probably be far more interesting and contain events of greater moment than all the three score years and ten that follow it.’

Thus wrote the oft-quoted Samuel Taylor Coleridge in 1802. That same fascination for the prenatal period has captured the imagination and interest of many and yet it is only within the last fifteen years or so that prenatal psychology and medicine has become a focal interest, in England at least. Prematurity and the special care setting has provided us with an opportunity to observe ‘the inside baby’ — outside.

Anne McFadyen's book on Special Care Babies and their Developing Relationships is an important and timely contribution and will, no doubt, become essential reading for all those who enter the fascinating world of the neonatal intensive care unit — a world in which babies are at the centre of a highly complex and multi-layered system of relationships comprising the family and the professionals who provide the care, located within the institutional hospital setting, itself in turn affected by the political climate of the day. This emphasis on the multi-layered complexity of the internal/external recurs throughout the book.

The book's structure and presentation in clearly defined sections is designed to allow the reader to engage with the material in his own way, either via clinical interest or from the theoretical and philosophical perspective.

This format is useful to both parents and professionals who struggle to survive the stressful experience and move beyond survival to find meaning in a setting in which constant exposure to extreme vulnerability, disability and death forms part of daily reality.

413

Eric: A Traumatized Child

Pat Radford

Pat Radford

Flat 2
14 Ferncroft Avenue
London NW3 7PH

Pat Radford  

Trauma, violence, child analysis,

I have undertaken in this paper to explore the traumatic effects of ongoing interpersonal violence on the developmental process of a 312-year-old boy. The clinical material is based on my psychoanalytic five times weekly treatment of Eric over a period of three years. His external environment, including the violent aspects of his family's life, is clarified. The supportive work which attempted to bring about environmental change is outlined. The lasting effects of the violence on Eric's personality and development are estimated, and the possible value to him of his psychoanalytic treatment is assessed.

Editorial

Anna Freud

Anna Freud

Anna Freud  

This special issue of the Journal marks the centenary of the birth of Anna Freud, the youngest of Sigmund Freud's six children. Born in Vienna on 3 December 1895, Miss Freud was educated at the Cottage Lyceum where she later taught for five years. Her first paper — on fantasy life in children — was written in 1922, gaining her membership of the Vienna Psychoanalytical Society which she chaired at the time of the Freud family's flight to London in 1938.

As well as stressing the influence of this early concern with education and child development on Anna Freud's future psychoanalytic career, contributions to this issue also point to the importance of her experience of attending, in Vienna, the psychiatric clinic run by Professor Wagner Jauregg and involving Paul Schilder and Heinz Hartmann: this connection between child development and adult disturbance was to remain a life-long fascination.

More difficult, perhaps, thirteen years after Anna Freud's death, is the expression of ambivalence about such a key figure in the psychoanalysis of children. Some of our authors touch on the pain of the ‘Controversial Discussions’; others hint at what her obituary in the Times of 11 October 1982 expressed more clearly: ‘She was generous in her recognition of the contributions of others but she never tolerated fools gladly. Her criticisms could be telling, forceful and, on occasion, annihilating.’ Throughout the papers in this issue, however, appear great admiration for her intellect, appreciation of her gifts as a teacher, her charm and humour, and the influence she had on her ‘qualified students’ as they continued her rigorous approach to theory, research and practice. Above all there emerges Anna Freud's commitment to the ‘best interests of the child’.

Memories

Memories Peter Wilson Director of Young Minds (the National Association for Child and Family Mental Health) recalls leaving the then Hampstead Clinic and the following encounter with Miss Freud.

In reading through the very many contributions offered for this section, we have been struck by the recurrence of several themes: first and foremost, Anna Freud's reputation as a teacher of exceptional talent; her intellectual strength; integrity; a continuing curiosity which was firmly rooted in the concept of ‘normality’, exploring from that as a secure base; a shy personality, socially uneasy with small talk, inclined to emotional reticence but capable of deep friendship and great grace; and, above all, someone committed to the internal — and external — health of children and young people. A dry and occasionally acerbic sense of humour is not far away, as our first contributor shows.

It was at that point in my life when it was time to move on; to make the break from the place that had brought me up and find my own place in the big wide world. Time, in fact, to leave the Anna Freud Centre (psychoanalysis) and enter the world of the Maudsley Hospital and the Institute of Psychiatry (academic, behavioural, cognitive). After ten or so years of childhood and adolescence, time now to grow up.

To ‘mother’ herself, I presented myself: my decision, my firm and courageous intention. A historic moment, none the less — not easy, not straightforward, not comfortable. Daunting, perhaps a better word. ‘Miss Freud,’ I said, ‘I have been offered important work in the Maudsley; I have decided to resign from the clinic.’

A quizzical look — head nodding, as it often did seemingly in sufferance, but with interest, if lack of comprehension. I hurried on, emphasizing the virtue of the new post and the value of everything I had learned.

‘Why is death longer than life?’ a 5-year-old boy, developing normally, asked his mother in the course of discussion about the circumstances of his grandfather's death before his birth. A question so simple and profound, related by the mother to this reviewer, touching the essentials of the human condition, encapsulates the topic of this collection of psychoanalytic papers, a topic at the heart of psychoanalytic theory and practice.

This is an ambitious volume, a collection whose declared aim is to bring together ‘the most significant contributions to psychoanalytic and psychological understanding of the effect of object loss on adults and children’. It aspires to lead to more focused attention in clinical work and teaching through this exploration of psychoanalytic works spanning eighty years (the earliest paper included is by Karl Abraham, 1911), a collection which examines not only fundamental distinctions between mourning and depression but the traumas occasioned by object loss, its nature, its characteristics and the obstacles to attachment that may be sequelae. Twenty-seven papers are grouped here in seven sections. Introductory notes by the editor, Rita V. Frankiel, are included and appear as introductions to individual papers, to groups of papers or to the separate sections.

This is a well-produced book and each individual paper has a full and accurate bibliography or a set of references (some of which are numbered, some not). In addition, at the end of the volume there appears a set of editor's references, and, also grouped in relation to the sections of the book, a set of highly recommended readings. This makes this volume a good source book but, read together, the twenty-seven papers, together with their editorial introduction and linking, provide a full and coherent overview of the topic and its historical, theoretical and applied dimensions. Through selection and introduction, the editor has created a coherence which makes this whole greater than the sum of its parts, although the parts are also valuable in themselves.

This book is a collection of papers by leading American clinicians and researchers. It is cleverly organized as it becomes a forum for discussion about the relationship between psychotherapy practice and psychotherapy research. Its main theme is the split between the two disciplines and the ongoing debate about the difficulty in making scientific enquiry about clinical issues that are known more ‘intuitively’ than intellectually.

In the first part of the book, psychoanalysts discuss and describe their views and concerns in relation to the split. Among them, Jay Greenberg states that ‘the gap between psychotherapy research and clinicians resists closure and threatens to widen’. He argues that it cannot be otherwise since they observe things from different perspectives and he takes to task the empiricist position of philosophers of science such as Grunbaun and his critique of psychoanalysis, that scientific procedures which are designed to establish validity, reliability, specific observational conditions and replicability cannot be applied to data collected by the analytic model. The relationship that develops is one in which therapists are insiders and researchers are sceptical outsiders.

Edelson creates a dialogue between himself and a researcher to illustrate the complexity of the psychoanalytic process. He views the case study as the patient's story and develops the idea of a corresponding unconscious ‘master story’. Within this study framework he illustrates that his enquiry does not preclude the formulation and testing of specific hypotheses, through noting significant observations within the here and now that would falsify his hypothesis.

Psychotherapy clinic; establishment; training; brief psychotherapy; concurrent therapy; Australia.

This paper describes the establishment of a fee-for-service, not for profit, psychotherapy clinic in a large paediatric teaching hospital in Australia. The establishment of such a clinic required simultaneous attention to a number of different fields, i.e. the clinical, organizational and training issues, complementing each other in the provision of the service. The paper goes on to describe the development of the concurrent therapy model in the clinic where two therapists are allocated for each case, one to see the child and one to see the parents. The child's presenting problem is thus viewed within the family context and as part of an interactive process. Clinical examples are given which identify the nature of the ‘shared fantasy’ between child and parents and show how dynamically this therapeutic model can work in developing insight and creating change for both child and parents, particularly in short-term, focused psychotherapy. The paper describes how the fee-for-service clinic developed as an entrepreneurial initiative within a large institution and the advantages of such a model for child psychotherapy services elsewhere which operate on the boundary between the public and private sectors.

The paper goes on to outline the development of an Associate Training Programme for paediatricians in the clinic which served to develop clinical skills in observation, assessment and treatment and which could be applied by paediatricians in their everyday practice.

Finally, a personal view is given of how some of the presenting clinical problems can be viewed within the broader Australian context.

Editorial

We are glad to present, as the first issue of 1995, an international issue with papers from Australia, Belgium, France and Italy. Although making this a special issue has perhaps encouraged authors from further afield to contribute, we hope that this flow of contributions will continue and that the Journal will achieve a regular international flavour as a matter of course. Thank you to all the many people who have sent in contributions.

It is a pleasure to announce in this issue that the Advisory Board has been joined by the eminent Hungarian psychoanalyst, psychiatrist and child psychiatrist Dr Georgy Vikar. Dr Vikar is a training analyst in the Hungarian Psychoanalytical Society in Budapest and we are delighted to receive his support and to develop connections with Hungary.

As this issue goes to press (in November 1994) we anticipate this month a fruitful Journal Annual General Meeting with members of the Advisory Board, representatives from Routledge, past editors, members of the ACP Executive and the Journal Editorial Committee. This, our first AGM, will be an annual event which we hope will stimulate more thinking on the development and direction of the Journal. It is also an opportunity to thank our Advisory Board members for their support throughout the year.

Papers in this issue represent a range of issues for child psychotherapists, but it is interesting that several of them focus on severely disturbed patients and very early experience.

The first paper in this issue focusing on very early experience is Alessandra Piontelli's account of the analysis of a 4-year-old psychotic adopted boy. Abandoned a few days after birth and then subjected to severe cumulative trauma, Antonino's development was seriously disturbed by the time he was adopted and started analysis. The description of the therapy highlights most vividly and poignantly how Antonino seemed to be trying desperately to recapture the sensory experience of attachment to his biological mother — the lost and abandoning primary object.

Valerie SinasonAnne Marie Sandler Director of the Anna Freud Centre from 1994

VS: When did you first meet Anna Freud and what impression did she make on you personally?

AMS: I first met Anna Freud in November 1950. I had somewhat belatedly arrived from Geneva to start the Hampstead Clinic training. My first visit was to Anna Freud. I was rather nervous about this visit and I had anxiously prepared myself to answer the many questions I expected to be asked about children and psychoanalysis. When I rang the bell at 20 Maresfield Gardens, Paula, the housekeeper, opened the door, and told me that Miss Freud was waiting for me on the first floor. Anna Freud greeted me very graciously, took me into her consulting room and commiserated about the very cold weather. She then started to speak a little bit about the work of the clinic and suddenly turned to me and asked in a concerned voice: ‘Are you wearing warm underwear? It is very important here with all the draughts and dampness of English houses!’

Anna Freud was genuinely concerned about people but she could give the impression of being distant or even haughty. I always felt that this was due to shyness. Anna Freud was a very private person and to us at the clinic she only showed her professional self.

For Anna Freud, to be a psychoanalytic child therapist or analyst was a work of dedication to the cause and so issues of salary and increments were not of interest to her. This made it very difficult for staff who had a young family. She also found it difficult to be sympathetic to a trainee who would become pregnant during her training. Her sympathy was with the patients who would be displaced and whose treatment would be interrupted.

On the other hand, her loyalty and generosity was substantial.

Before I left for Israel she invited me to 20 Maresfield Gardens. I was convinced I was leaving England for good and I found this extremely difficult. She knew it and was very kind and supportive, refusing to let me step down from the training committee of the clinic.

This paper describes the three-year treatment of a boy with speech difficulties who had been born prematurely and whose early life was characterized by repeated medical interventions. Iris Gibbs  

This book is a welcome addition to the literature on this controversial subject. It comprises six chapters, each by a different author, embracing different perspectives — personal, historical, legal, political, psychological. The authors’ interests stem from their involvement in the group Children First in transracial fostering and adoption. Their abiding concerns are both for children who wait for permanent families and for the well-being of existing transracial families. All the authors are unequivocal in supporting the view that black children should be placed with black families wherever possible; nevertheless they believe there comes a point when the advantages of this have to be weighed against the costs to the child's need for a permanent family.

The text draws on research studies like Rowe and Lambert's Children who Wait which showed that the longer the child waited for placement, the less likely s/he was to return to family life, and on the longitudinal results of the work of Simon and Alstein (1977, 1981, 1987) which showed that transracial placements are satisfactory substitutes in the absence of same-race placements. These latter studies gave little support for criticisms of transracial placements based on anticipated difficulties later in life. The difficulties foreseen by critics of such placements included poor survival skills in a racist society, inability to relate either to black or to white, lack of racial pride and dilution of identity, thus undercutting the prospect of a positive black identity. In essence these placements were seen by critics as amounting to ‘internal colonialism’, cultural genocide, exploitation, repression and the perpetuation of a racist ideology. The influential group of black social workers and allied professions (ABSWAP) were and remain severe critics of these placements, unanimously condemning such studies as Gill and Jackson (1983) who described them as largely successful despite their description of some of the children as ‘white’ in all but skin colour. ABSWAP drew support for their views from such studies as Chestang (1972), an American theorist who argued that the black child's psycho-survival is paramount and can be obtained only in the black community.

Kin Recognition and Early Precursors of Attachment as Seen in the Analysis of a Young Psychotic Adopted Boy

Alessandra Piontelli

Alessandra Piontelli

Largo Richini 1
20122 Milan
Italy

Alessandra Piontelli  

Biological mother; adoption; psychosis; abandonment; child analysis.

This paper describes some features of the behaviour in analysis of a young psychotic adopted boy who had been abandoned by his natural mother when he was only a few days old. Though his subsequent development had been heavily clouded by a number of horrifying and tragic events, this boy seemed to be hanging on to some kind of memory of the sensuous qualities of his primary object and searched frantically for them in all the women that he met. Yet their smell, voice and taste never quite seemed to match that of the original object which he had irretrievably lost.

Recent research on early kin recognition appears to throw some light upon the behaviour of this young boy in analysis. Current research on kin recognition relevant to the understanding of this particular case is reported and discussed. Some reflections of a more general nature regarding the possible development of kin recognition and early precursors of attachment both pre- and peri-natally, as well as on adoption in general, are discussed at the end.

Suzanne Maiello

Via Dalmazia 18A

Suzanne Maiello  

Prenatal experience; sound; separation; psychotherapy.

The exploration of the area of possible prenatal experience suggests that the sound of the mother's voice, alternating with silence, may give the child a proto-experience of both presence and absence. This experience may, on the one hand, give rise to primitive defensive reactions and, on the other, become the basis for the constitution of a prenatal proto-object with sound qualities called tentatively ‘sound-object’. The hypothesis is made that this object could be connected with the preconception of the breast, and could also be considered as a precursor of the postnatal maternal inner object.

Two dreams of adults and clinical material of a child patient are examined with special attention to sound aspects and their possible connection with prenatal experiences. The importance of integrating sound aspects, especially in analytic work with borderline and psychotic patients, is discussed.

Precipitation Anxiety

Didier Houzel

Didier Houzel

6 rue de l'Académie
14000 Caen
France

Didier Houzel  

Anxiety, autism, object relationships, birth,

Therapy with autistic and psychotic children led the author to introduce the concept of precipitation anxiety. Freud's first theory of the instincts was expressed in the dynamics of conflict, but his subsequent development of life and death instincts is better understood in terms of a gradient of energy between two extremities of the same axis. Object relations result from a caesura (Bion) which creates a gradient of psychic energy experienced initially as a precipice which, if left unregulated, generates intolerable anxiety. Satisfactory emotional encounters with the mind of the object bring about the necessary adjustments to the slope of the gradient. Autistic mechanisms may block off precipitation anxiety, but they also prevent mental growth. Both the dynamics of conflict and the dynamics of the gradient are vital for psychic development, but the very existence of the former is contingent on successful negotiation of the energy gradient (working through). After illustrating his thesis with clinical material drawn from a group therapeutic setting, the author discusses points of convergence and divergence with two other fundamental notions: the aesthetic conflict (Meltzer) and premature psychic birth (Tustin). The proposed model furthers our understanding of the therapeutic process and stresses the importance of the containing object in the transference situation.

Motiveless Malignity: Problems in the Psychotherapy of Psychopathic Patients

Anne Alvarez

Anne Alvarez

Tavistock Clinic
120 Belsize Lane
London NW3 5BA

Anne Alvarez  

Psychopathy, violence, technique, psychotherapy,

This paper attempts to draw attention to the difference between the states of mind and inner worlds of neurotic, borderline and psychopathic patients, with reference to different types of destructiveness: anger in the neurotic patient; desperate vengeful hatred in the borderline paranoid; and a cold addiction to violence in the psychopath. Discussion focuses on technical issues and the need to meet the psychopathic patient where he really is, in the inner bleak emotional cemetery he may be inhabiting. Although most patients refuse to stay put in the neat schematic categories outlined, they do seem to appreciate and to need the therapist's recognition of the specific quality of these vastly different states of mind.

Leslie Ironside

Leslie Ironside

35 Clermont Terrace
Brighton BN1 6SJ

Leslie Ironside  

False allegations, sexual abuse, psychotherapy,

This paper explores the difficult clinical situation when a child makes a false allegation of sexual abuse against a therapist. The experience of an allegation being acted upon, involving the child's withdrawal from therapy and full child protection procedures, is contrasted with three cases where it was not found necessary to follow that protocol. Aspects of the child's pathology and history are shown to blur the distinction between acting-out and remembering, to lead to concrete rather than symbolic thinking, and comment is made on early primitive mechanisms and anxieties overlaid by experiences of neglect and abuse. Factors in the child are paralleled in the response of the network, with consequent increased vulnerability of the therapist. Difficulties of containment and issues in continuing therapy are explored.

As Jeremy Holmes himself proclaims, this book is intended to be more than just a biography of psychoanalyst and scientist John Bowlby. While offering a comprehensive summary of attachment theory and research, there is also a distinctive synthesizing process at work which makes this a unique compilation of theoretical concepts, research findings, clinical vignettes and biography set in historical and socio-cultural context. The book is written in a straightforward, creative and flowing style which makes for a titillating read. Holmes’ enthusiasm for John Bowlby and his work is clear, yet there is critical evaluation as well which serves to keep this from becoming a shrine to Bowlby. The possible audience who might appreciate this work is wide, including not only the psychotherapist but also the developmental psychologist, psychiatric social worker and sociologist among others. The underlying message is one aimed particularly at the psychotherapeutic community — a message to consider attachment theory and research as a paramount source of information and support to effective work in the consulting-room.

The book is organized into three sections: Origins, Attachment Theory and Implications. In ‘Origins’ one is invited to consider Bowlby's own attachment history in terms of its significance for his work. There is something mischievous in the air as one is invited to page through Bowlby's life in a candid fashion that makes one feel privy to that which is most often left off-limits, especially since we are also told that John Bowlby was ‘notoriously reticent’ about his background.

This book is unusual in that it gives an up to date, comprehensive account of the development of Kleinian thinking and practice in a comparatively short volume. Yet it is by no means a ‘potted’ version of Klein. It earns its title by the presentation of a series of clinical vignettes, in more or less chronological sequence, from Melanie Klein's earliest writings, to her later work and that of her followers, especially Segal, Rosenfeld, Bion and Betty Joseph. The author intends the present volume with its clinical emphasis to complement his more theoretical Dictionary of Kleinian Thought (1988). Thus it differs from earlier introductions and expositions of Klein (Segal, 1964; Meltzer, 1978) in its wide span of clinical material from a variety of analysts, including later developments in Kleinian practice and technique highlighted by Spillius (1988). In its method of approach it has something in common with Wittenberg's Psychoanalytic Insight and Relationships (1970), for it illustrates key Kleinian concepts by means of clinical material.

The experience of reading this book was for me the mental equivalent of a challenging mountain climb, steep but exhilarating. It rewarded me en route both with views of familiar terrain, seen from different perspectives, and with vast new landscapes. When I began to flag, the figure of Henri Rey, the exuberant teacher, seemed to beckon me ever

404

onwards, pointing out the complex links between his vast clinical experience and the range of theoretical thinking he draws on to explain and describe mental phenomena. Yet, having struggled to reach the summit, I found that some of the scenery remained hidden from view, shrouded in a mist of confusion and leaving me frustrated and tantalized by what I felt I was missing. The journey is best undertaken at a leisurely pace, with pauses to take in the expansive panorama.

This volume is a compilation of Henry Rey's writings, spanning at least thirty years of research and clinical work. The eighteen chapters cover a diverse and fascinating range of subjects but the core of his work is the elaboration of his original ideas about the structuring of the internal world of borderline and psychotic patients. The additional sub-title ‘Factors of Space-Time and Language’ hints at the weighty intellectual matter within, and announces Rey's central preoccupations. These concern the relationship between the infant's early construction of external and internal reality (according to Piaget), and how these early constructs of space and time relate to the development of language and thought. In turn, Rey shows how these primitive concepts of space and time can help us to understand the mental experiences of borderline/psychotic patients, whose confused and unstable sense of identity in space and time resembles those early stages of childhood development.

In Chapter 2, ‘The schizoid mode of being’, Rey describes Piaget's ideas on the early organization of space, movement and time in infancy and early childhood, and applies these to the world of his borderline psychotic patients in an attempt to describe their subjective experience. These patients suffer from severe distortions in their perceptions of reality, disorientations in space and time and claustro/agoraphobia. In a lengthy, rather tortuous section, Rey describes Piaget's work on early cognitive stages of development. The child goes through distinct cognitive stages in developing a sense of permanence of himself (stable identity) and of his objects. Through his well-known experiments Piaget has demonstrated that, for example, a child's concept of ‘conservation of quantity’ takes some time to develop: when showing a child the same amount of water in a tall thin tube and a shorter wider container, he will say there is more water in the tall thin tube, because his sense of the constancy of matter is not strongly developed and can easily be swayed by his perception of spatial differences. Therefore, on a cognitive level, the child inhabits a fluctuating, unstable world, although this is separate from and not to be confused with his emotional development and sense of object constancy in the psychoanalytic sense.

Pam Schein  

Premature, mothers of premature babies, psychic functioning,

This paper is a group's case study of a mother when her infant is prematurely born by caesarean section and there is danger of death to both. The group's thinking is tentative and hopefully inviting of further thinking by the readers. For us this was a unique opportunity to share Deedie's (the mother's) firsthand experience of a sensitive and traumatic time. We came to understand that her awakening from an emotional deadness did not return her to a normal state, but led to a revival of the earliest primitive template of her psychic functioning. Covering the first three months of her infant's life, we see the changes in her inner world from an affectless state of shock to an enactment of her most primitive fears and impulses as she struggles towards motherhood. We hope this paper goes some way towards showing the special challenge for the mother whose infant is in neonatal intensive care.
